explainers.title: Hello again, and welcome to Evaluation
explainers.body:
Hello, and welcome back to Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. You have already grown two thinking skills this year. In Research you learned to find out about the world in a careful way. In Analysis you learned to look closely at a topic and ask why things happen. Now you are ready for the third skill: Evaluation.

Here are all six thinking skills again, so you can see where this unit fits:

In Research you gathered lots of sources. A source is anywhere your information comes from: a book, a website, a video, an advert, or a person who knows. But here is the thing. Not every source is worth using. Some are helpful, some are old, and some are only trying to sell you something. Evaluation is the skill of weighing a source, so you know how much to trust it.

Think of it like choosing fruit at a market. You do not drop every mango into your basket. You pick each one up, look it over, and keep the good ones. Evaluation teaches you to do the very same thing with information.
bullets: Research — finding out about the world in a careful way.
Analysis — looking closely at a topic and asking why things happen.
Evaluation — deciding how good, useful or trustworthy something really is.
Reflection — thinking about how you learn and how you change your mind.
Collaboration — working well with other people.
Communication — sharing your ideas so others understand.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You learn in the Ehel Academy way. Three kinds of help work together:

In the old way of this subject, children were told to 'talk to a partner' or 'talk as a class'. In our way, your AI tutor is your partner and your class. Evaluation loves a good chat, because talking about a source out loud helps you spot what is good and what is weak about it. So every time you see an 'Ask Your AI Tutor' box, have a real chat with it.

Your evaluation skill will grow in three steps this year, like a young tree. First you are starting the skill. Then you are developing it. Then you are getting better at it. Do not worry if judging a source feels tricky at first. Starting is meant to feel like a first try.
bullets: You, at your own speed. You read, think and do the activities in your own time. You can go slowly on a hard part, or quickly on an easy one.

Your AI tutor, ready any time, day or night. When this book says 'Ask Your AI Tutor', you talk to your tutor like a friendly helper. It will chat about your ideas, kindly disagree with you, and answer your questions at any hour.
Your teacher, about twice a week. In your live sessions you share your best work and ask your biggest questions.

explainers.title: Meet Nadia, our evaluator for this unit
explainers.body:
To make each skill clear, we will follow one Year 4 learner all the way through. Her name is Nadia, and she is a pupil at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa.

One lunchtime, Nadia looks at the food on her plate: some anjero, a spoon of beans, a banana, and a juicy mango. She starts to wonder about it. Where did each food come from? Who grew it? How did it reach her plate? And how much did it really cost, in money and in hard work? That is when a big question pops into her head: what does my lunch cost?

That question becomes Nadia's own project for this unit. At the same time, her whole class at Ehel Academy is doing a project together, comparing schools and education here in Hargeisa and in other countries. As Nadia meets each new evaluation skill, she will use it on both: on the sources for her lunch question, and on the sources her class is studying about schools. You will do the very same thing, with a topic that matters to you.

explainers.title: Your Challenge: What does my lunch cost?
explainers.body: Amara is curious about the long trip that dates and flour take by ship to Berbera port, then by truck to markets in Hargeisa.
bullets: A seller at the Hargeisa market who knows where the fruit comes from.
A bright advert for a sugary mango juice.
A website about a farm that grows mangoes and bananas.
A newspaper story about the price of rice and dates in the markets.

explainers.title: So what is evaluation?
explainers.body:
In everyday life, to evaluate something means to study it carefully and decide how good or how useful it is. In Global Perspectives, evaluation means thinking carefully about the sources you use, who made them, and what their ideas are. It also means giving your own opinion about what another person thinks, and saying clearly why you agree or disagree.

When you evaluate a source, you really do three things, and this unit teaches all three:

Notice that evaluation is not just calling a source 'good' or 'bad'. It is more careful than that. The clever trick is to ask three little questions about every source. Keep them close, because you will use them again and again.
bullets: Look at a source and talk about the ideas it gives about an issue.
Decide how useful and trustworthy the source is, by asking who made it and why.
Give your own opinion about other people's ideas, and always give a reason why.

explainers.title: Starting with evaluation
explainers.body: In the first two lessons you are just starting this skill. Two goals guide you here: to talk about a source and the ideas it gives about an issue, and to give reasons for your opinion. Let us begin with the most useful skill of all: telling a fact from an opinion.

explainers.title: Fact and opinion
explainers.body: Sources are full of two different things, and a good evaluator can tell them apart. A factual claim is something that can be checked against reliable evidence. An opinion is what someone thinks or believes, which other people may not agree with.
bullets: Fact: a mango has a large seed in the middle. You can check this by cutting one open.
Opinion: mangoes are the nicest fruit in the world. Someone else could easily disagree.

explainers.title: Talking about a source: is it relevant?
explainers.body:
When you research a question, you pick up many sources. But not every source helps with your question. A source that is really about your question is relevant. A source that is about something else is not relevant, even if it is interesting.

So a smart evaluator always asks: does this source actually answer my question?

explainers.title: Which source is the most useful?
explainers.body: Often you have a few sources about the same thing, and you must choose the most useful one. To do this, you ask who made each source, why they made it, and whether it gives real evidence (facts you can check) or just an opinion.

explainers.title: Giving reasons for your opinion
explainers.body:
When you share what you think, you must always give a reason. An opinion with no reason is weak. An opinion with a good reason is strong, and people listen to it.

It also helps to look at more than one perspective. A perspective is a way of seeing something. Different people can look at the same issue and see it in different ways.

explainers.title: Developing evaluation
explainers.body: Now you are developing the skill. In the next two lessons you go deeper. You learn to talk about who wrote a source and discuss the author's ideas, and to give reasons for your opinion about other people's ideas, not just about the issue.

explainers.title: Who made it, and why?
explainers.body:
The very first question a good evaluator asks is 'who?'. The person or group who made a source is called the author or creator. Knowing who made a source, and whether they really know the topic, tells you a lot about how far to trust it.

It also helps to ask why they made it. Some authors want to inform you, which means to give you facts. Some want to persuade you, which means to make you agree or buy something. Both can be useful, but you read them differently.

explainers.title: Is a source useful for taking action?
explainers.body: Sometimes people do not just want to know about an issue. They want to do something about it. So you ask a sharper question: is this source useful for taking action? And inside each source, you can still hunt for one fact and one opinion.

explainers.title: Perspectives: for and against, and what you think
explainers.body: On many issues, people are split. Some are for an idea and some are against it. A strong evaluator can spot each perspective, work out who might hold it and why, and then give a fair opinion about it, with reasons.

explainers.title: Getting better at evaluation
explainers.body: In the last lesson you start getting better at the skill. Now you weigh a source's strengths and limitations, and you judge how trustworthy it is. You also learn one clever, surprising idea about sources you cannot fully trust.

explainers.title: Strengths and limitations
explainers.body:
No source is perfect. Every source has strengths, the things it is good at, and limitations, the things it is not good at or cannot tell you. A skilled evaluator names both, instead of just saying 'I like it' or 'I do not like it'.

A good way to do this is to sort an author's ideas into two columns: strengths on one side, limitations on the other.

explainers.title: Is it trustworthy? A clever surprise
explainers.body:
The heart of evaluation is deciding how far to trust a source. A trustworthy source is one you can believe, because it is fair and made by someone who really knows. To decide, you weigh the strengths and limitations you found, and you ask if the author has any reason to trick you.

But here is a clever surprise that many people get wrong. Some children think this: 'an untrustworthy source is never useful.' That is not quite right. Even a source you cannot fully trust can still be useful, because it can show you a perspective, or show you how someone tries to persuade.

explainers.title: How evaluation helps the other five skills
explainers.body:
Evaluation is the third Global Perspectives skill, and it helps all the others.

So the care you take in evaluation now is never wasted. It makes every other skill sharper.
bullets: Research gives you the sources; evaluation decides which ones are worth using.
Analysis breaks an idea into parts; evaluation judges how strong that idea really is.
Reflection grows every time you notice how a source, or your tutor, changed your mind.
Collaboration works better when you can weigh other people's ideas fairly, without falling out.
Communication is stronger when you back your message with sources you have judged to be trustworthy.

explainers.title: Putting it all together
explainers.body: You have now met every evaluation skill in this unit. Here is the whole journey in simple steps you can use for any source:
bullets: Ask who made the source, and why.
Sort what it says into facts and opinions.
Ask if the source is relevant and useful for your question.
Weigh its strengths and its limitations.
Decide how far you trust it, and say what you think, with a reason.

explainers.title: What comes next
explainers.body: The next unit is Reflection. Once you can evaluate sources and other people's ideas, reflection teaches you to turn that same careful, fair thinking on yourself: how you learn, how you changed your mind, and what you will do better next time. Strong evaluation now makes strong reflection easy later. Well done for growing a skill that will keep you wise for the rest of your life.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to remember
lines: In Global Perspectives, the topic is like a bus, and the skill is where the bus takes you.
We will use real topics, like the food in our lunch and how schools work.
But the real prize is to become someone who can look at any source and decide, calmly, how far to trust it.

bigIdeas.title: The three questions an evaluator asks
lines: Who made this source? Was it an expert who really knows, someone sharing their own experience, or a person just giving an opinion?
What are their ideas for? Do they want to inform you (give you facts), or persuade you (make you agree or buy something)?
What do other people think? Which ideas do I agree with, and why? Which do I disagree with, and why?

bigIdeas.title: An untrustworthy source can still be useful
lines: Some people think a source you cannot trust is never worth keeping. That is not quite right.
A biased advert cannot be trusted for facts, but it can still show you how sellers try to persuade.
So do not always throw a weak source away. Sometimes it is useful to understand a perspective, as long as you keep your eyes open.

bigIdeas.title: Your Challenge runs through everything
lines: Your Challenge is Nadia's question: what does my lunch cost?
You will gather a few sources about the food you eat, and evaluate each one.
By the end you will be able to say who to trust, what your food really costs, and why.

bigIdeas.title: The three sources, described
lines: Source 1: Bright Star School's own web page. It says: small classes are best, and no class here is bigger than fifteen children!
Source 2: a teachers' opinion site. It says: most teachers believe smaller classes help — but is this really true?
Source 3: a statistics website. It shows the real average class size in many different countries.

bigIdeas.title: Two head teachers speak
lines: Green Hill School: We start at 7:15 in the morning. We have had no complaints in years.
Riverside School: We start at 10 in the morning. Students and teachers welcome it, and the place feels full of life.

bigIdeas.title: The two letters, in short
lines: Mr Adams thinks the plan is unfair. His main reason: his daughter has no computer at home. His evidence: she fell behind last term.
Mrs Silva likes the plan. Her main reason: her son concentrates better at home. Her evidence: his reading improved.

models.title: Evaluation happens at the market too
lines: Nadia's friend says the stall by the gate sells the sweetest mangoes in Hargeisa.
Nadia does not just believe it at once. She asks herself: does my friend really know? Has she tried many stalls, or only this one?
Then a sign on the stall says exactly the same thing. Nadia trusts the sign less, because the seller wrote it to sell mangoes.
Weighing her friend and the sign, and deciding who to trust, is real evaluation. Nadia already does it.
So evaluation is not a strange, school-only thing. In this unit you will simply learn to do it on purpose, with more skill.

models.title: Nadia reads a school advert
lines: Nadia's class looks at an advert for a made-up school called Sunrise Academy.
It says: Sunrise Academy opened in 2015. That is a fact, because you could check it.
It says: Sunrise Academy is the best school in all of Hargeisa. That is an opinion, because other people could disagree.
It says: every child here is sure to succeed. That is an opinion too, dressed up to sound like a promise.
Nadia sees that the advert mixes a few facts with lots of shiny opinions, to make families want to choose the school.

models.title: Nadia's class matches sources to questions
lines: The class wants to know about schools in another country. Their questions are: at what age do children start school? at what age do they leave? how many hours a week are they in school?
A source called Starting School in Kenya answers the first question, so it is relevant.
A source called The School Week in Japan answers the hours question, so it is relevant too.
But a source called The Best Football Teams in the World does not answer any school question. It is interesting, but it is not relevant here.

models.title: Three sources about class size
lines: Malik looks up class size and finds three results online.
One is Bright Star School's own web page. It says: our small classes are best, no class is bigger than 15! Its purpose is to sell the school, so Malik is careful.
One is a teachers' opinion site. It says: most teachers believe smaller classes help — but is that really true? This gives opinions, not proof.
One is a statistics website that compares the real average class size in many countries. It gives facts and is not selling anything.
Malik decides the statistics website is the most useful, because it gives evidence he can trust.

models.title: Two head teachers, two perspectives on start time
lines: Two newspapers print different views on what time school should start.
The head teacher of Green Hill School says: we start at 7:15 in the morning, and we have had no complaints in years.
The head teacher of Riverside School says: we start at 10 in the morning, and students and teachers welcome it — the place feels full of life.

Nadia sees who supports each view and what evidence each one gives. Then she gives her own opinion, with a reason: I think a later start is better, because children who sleep enough can concentrate more.

models.title: Amara chooses a book by its blurb
lines: Amara is researching fair access to computers in schools. She finds three books and reads the few sentences on the back of each.
One is a retired teacher's memoir about fifty years in the classroom. It has real experience, but it may be a little out of date about new technology.
One is by an education researcher who studies how new technology helps children learn. This author knows exactly this topic.
One is by a journalist writing about rivers and forests. That is interesting, but it is not about computers at all.
Amara chooses the researcher's book, because the author's job is the very thing she is studying.

models.title: Sources for a home-study decision
lines: A school is half-closed for building work, so children can only attend two days a week and study at home the rest. Parents want to act.
A newspaper report called Home or School? looks at the real issue and gives facts and views. It is useful.
Adverts for home tutoring give some help, but they are trying to sell lessons, so Layla reads them with care.
A leisure-centre website about swimming times is not useful at all here, because it is about something else.
In the newspaper report, Layla underlines one fact (many children share one computer at home) and one opinion (children learn best at school).

models.title: Who is for and against school uniform?
lines: The class sorts what different people say about wearing a school uniform.
I sell uniforms in my shop — so this person is for uniform, because they would make money.
I love choosing my own clothes to show who I am — so this person is against uniform, because they value their own style.
Chasing the latest fashions costs too much — so this parent is for uniform, because it saves money and waste.
Omar works out who might say each one and why, then gives his own view with a reason.
When you say what you think of another person's idea, be exact. Do not just say 'I disagree'. Say what you disagree with, and why. That is the mark of a careful evaluator.

models.title: Nadia reads two parents' letters
lines: Two parents write to the school about the two-days-a-week home-study plan.
Mr Adams thinks the plan is unfair. His main reason is that his daughter has no computer at home. His evidence is that she fell behind last term.
Mrs Silva likes the plan. Her main reason is that her son concentrates better at home. Her evidence is that his reading improved.
Nadia says: I agree with Mr Adams that it is unfair for children with no computer, but I can see Mrs Silva's point too, so the school should lend computers to those who need them.

models.title: Sorting an author's ideas about home learning
lines: The class reads an author's argument about learning at home, and sorts the ideas.
A strength: computers let us learn anywhere, you cannot deny it. This is a strong, clear point.
A limitation: the writer just says children learn by playing, but never says how or why. That is not explained.
A limitation: the writer says classrooms are old-fashioned, but that is too general — some classrooms now have smart technology.
A strength: the writer gives real examples from three schools, which makes the point stronger.

models.title: Two food sources, and a surprising use
lines: Nadia compares two sources about mango juice.
A farming website gives facts about how mangoes grow. It is fair and trustworthy.
A bright juice advert says the drink is the healthiest choice ever. That is not trustworthy, because the company wants to sell it.
But the advert is still useful in one way: it shows Nadia exactly how sellers try to make sugary juice look healthy. So she keeps it, with her eyes open.

models.title: Nadia's whole journey, from lunch to answer
lines: Nadia asked who made each food source and why: a market seller, a farmer's website, and a juice advert.
She sorted facts from opinions, and saw the advert was mostly shiny opinions.
She checked which sources were relevant and useful for her question about cost.
She weighed each source's strengths and limitations, and judged how far to trust it.
She gave her opinion with a reason: my lunch costs more than the money price, because of the long work and travel to grow and bring the food.

By following these steps, Nadia turned a simple question about her lunch into a fair, well-thought-out answer she can share. In the Activities file, you will do the same with your own Challenge, one small step at a time, with your AI tutor beside you.

models.title: A model: fact or opinion?
lines: Sunrise Academy opened in 2015: this is a fact, because you could check the date.
Sunrise Academy is the best school in Hargeisa: this is an opinion, because other people could disagree.
Both sentences are about the same school. The difference is only whether they can be checked.
Then think about your own school. Write down two facts about it, and one opinion. Notice how different they feel.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Say hello to your AI tutor. Tell it: I am starting Unit 3 of Global Perspectives, and the skill is Evaluation.
Ask it: in one or two simple sentences, why is it useful to decide whether you can trust a source?
Then tell your tutor about a time you saw an advert or a poster that you did not quite believe, and why.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor, in your own words, what you think evaluation means now.
Ask it: is my idea missing anything important?
Then ask your tutor to give you one everyday example of evaluation that has nothing to do with school.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor two things about your own school: one fact and one opinion.
Ask it to check that you have sorted them the right way.
Then ask: why do adverts like to use opinions that sound like facts?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor one question from your lunch Challenge, such as where your rice comes from.
Describe one source you have, and ask: is this source relevant to my question, or is it about something else?
Then ask the tutor to suggest one more relevant source you could look for.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about two sources you have for your Challenge.
Ask it to help you decide which one is more useful, and why.
Then ask: which of my sources is only trying to sell me something?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Ask your AI tutor to tell you two different views on a school question, such as when school should start.
Say which view you agree with, and give one clear reason.
Then ask the tutor to argue the other side, and see if it changes your mind.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe one source for your Challenge to your AI tutor: who made it, and what you think they know about the topic.
Ask it to help you decide if the author wanted to inform you or persuade you.
Then ask: what is one thing I still do not know about who made this source?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor an action you might suggest for your Challenge, such as buying more local fruit.
Ask it which of your sources would be most useful to help you take that action.
Then ask the tutor to help you find one fact and one opinion inside that source.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Ask your AI tutor to give you two different views on a food question, such as whether school should sell sugary juice.
Say what you agree with, and what you disagree with, and give a reason for each.
Then ask the tutor who might hold each view, and why they might think that way.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe one source for your Challenge to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you name one strength and one limitation of that source.
Then ask: for my question, does the strength matter more, or the limitation?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about one source you would not fully trust, and say why.
Ask it: even so, could this source still be useful to me in any way?
Then ask the tutor to help you decide which of two sources is more trustworthy, and why.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your food and the sources you have so far.
Ask it: are these sources a good mix, or are they all the same kind?
Ask the tutor to suggest one more kind of source you could look for.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your six answers to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Then read your two facts and one opinion about your own school.
Ask the tutor: why does the advert use so many opinions that sound like promises?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your pairs to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Tell it which source was not relevant, and how you knew.
Then ask: which of these sources matches something I would like to know, and why?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your four answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether it would choose the same most-useful source as you.
Then ask the tutor: could the school's own page still be useful in any way?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your opinion on school start time, with your reason.
Ask it to argue the other side as strongly as it can.
Then tell the tutor your idea for changing a local school, and ask if your reason is clear and your result makes sense.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your choice and your reason to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether the author's job makes a book more trustworthy for this question.
Then ask: for my own Challenge, who would be the best author to trust, and why?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three judgements to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether the tutoring adverts might be a little biased, and why.
Then ask the tutor to help you spot a fact and an opinion in one of your own Challenge sources.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your sorting and your ideas about who says each one to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your reasons make sense.
Then tell the tutor your own opinion, and ask it to challenge you with the opposite view.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether you said exactly what you agree and disagree with, and gave a reason.
Then ask the tutor to be one of the parents, so you can practise replying kindly and clearly.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your sorting of A to D to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Then read the strengths and limitations of your two sources.
Ask the tutor: which of my two sources should I trust more, and could the other one still be useful?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three Challenge sentences to your AI tutor.
Ask it: from my evaluation, what is one fair thing I could tell my class about the cost of food?
Ask the tutor to help me plan how to share my findings with my teacher.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your stronger evaluations and your corrected labels to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your rewrites now name a strength or a limitation and give a reason.
Ask the tutor to show you one more way to reword any answer you found hard.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your five answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to tell you which answer was your strongest, and why.
Ask the tutor to give you one more question like these to try.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your reflection answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you notice how your thinking changed from the start of the unit to now.
Ask the tutor which evaluation skill to keep practising in the next unit, and why.

speakingPrompts.title: A human touch
lines: Ask someone at home about one food you often eat, such as rice, mangoes or anjero.
Where does it come from? Do they know who grows it, or how far it travels?
Bring their answer, and your own ideas, to your next teacher session.

speakingPrompts.title: Bring it to your teacher
lines: Save your idea for changing a local school: what you would change, why, and the result.
Share it in your next teacher session, and hear how other learners would change their school.

toolkit.title: The evaluation steps at a glance
toolkit.intro: Whatever your source, good evaluation follows the same steps. Come back to this list whenever you feel lost.
items: Who and why: find who made the source and why.
Fact or opinion: sort what it says.
Relevant and useful: is it really about my question, and does it help?
Strengths and limitations: weigh what it is good at and not good at.
Trust and think: decide how far to trust it, and say what I think, with a reason.

toolkit.title: What is evaluation?
toolkit.intro:
Evaluation means thinking carefully about a source to decide how useful and trustworthy it is. You do this by asking who made it and why, sorting facts from opinions, weighing its strengths and limitations, and giving your own opinion about it, with a reason.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, never just call a source 'good' or 'bad'; ask 'useful for what?'. Second, be fair: notice a source's side and weigh it with your eyes open, instead of believing it or throwing it away at once. If you remember nothing else, remember those two habits.

toolkit.title: A one-minute check for any source
toolkit.intro: When you do not have much time, run this fast check. It catches most problems in under a minute.
items: Who made it, and do they really know the topic?
Why did they make it: to inform me, or to sell me something?
Fact or opinion: is it something I could check, or just what they think?
Relevant: is it really about my question, or only near it?
So what: how far will I trust it, and how will I use it?

toolkit.title: Your Stage 4 Evaluation learning goals
toolkit.intro: Your evaluation skill grows in three stages this year. Here are your real goals for each stage, in simple words. It is fine to be working on any stage.

toolkit.title: Checker: is it a fact or an opinion?
toolkit.intro:
Sort what a source says. Facts and opinions both matter, but they do different jobs.

Opinion clue words such as best, worst, should, lovely or terrible are a sign you are reading an opinion, not a fact. When you spot one, slow down and ask whether the source can prove it.

rows: Can be checked and shown to be true.
What someone thinks; others may disagree.
This is the best school in town.

toolkit.title: Frame: strengths and limitations
toolkit.intro:
A strong evaluation always names both. Draw two columns and sort the author's ideas into them.

When you can name at least one strength and one limitation, you have truly weighed a source, instead of just reacting to it. Almost every source has some of each.

rows: It is clear and easy to understand.
It was made by someone who knows the topic.
It gives real examples or facts you can check.
The maker has something to gain.
It is closely about my question.
It is only near my question, not really about it.

toolkit.title: Giving your opinion about someone's idea
toolkit.intro:
When you hear another person's idea, say what you think, and always give a reason. Be exact: say what you agree or disagree with, not just 'I agree' or 'I disagree'.

Sentence starters you can use:
items: I can see why ... thinks that, but I ...
One strength of this idea is ..., but one limitation is ...

toolkit.title: The clever surprise about trust
toolkit.intro: Some people think a source you cannot trust is never worth keeping. That is not quite right. A biased advert cannot be trusted for facts, but it can still show you how sellers try to persuade. So do not always throw a weak source away. Sometimes it is useful to understand a perspective, as long as you keep your eyes open.

checklists.title: Checklist: who made this source, and why?
checklists.intro: The first evaluation question is always 'who?'. Then ask 'why?'. This checklist helps you work out who an author is and what they want. Then ask about their purpose. Some authors want to inform you, which means to give you facts. Others want to persuade you, which means to make you agree or buy something. An advert almost always wants to persuade, so read it with extra care.

checklists.title: Checklist: is it useful, relevant and trustworthy?
checklists.intro: Run these three quick checks on any source before you lean on it. A quick way to test trust is to ask one thing: would the maker lose anything by telling the whole truth? If yes, such as a company selling a drink, read the source with extra care.

challenge.intro: Start your Challenge about the cost of your lunch. You cannot evaluate sources you do not have, so first gather a small handful. Your sources do not need to be perfect. In fact, a mix of strong and weak sources makes this unit more fun, because your whole job is to tell them apart.
topics: Write your Challenge question in one sentence, such as: 'What does my lunch really cost?'
Choose one food you often eat, such as rice, mangoes, anjero or beans.
List three or four sources you could use, such as a market seller, an advert, a farming website, or an older person who has grown food.
checkpoints: The most useful source I found was ..., because ...
One source I decided not to fully trust was ..., because ...
After evaluating my sources, I now think my lunch costs ..., because ...

activities.title: Fact or opinion in a school advert
activities.label: Activity 2: Fact or opinion in a school advert
activities.intro: A fact can be checked and shown to be true. An opinion is what someone thinks, which others may not agree with. Read the made-up advert below. Write F for fact or O for opinion next to each letter.
steps: A. Sunrise Academy opened in the year 2015.
B. Sunrise Academy is the best school in all of Hargeisa.
C. The school day runs from 7:30 in the morning until 1:30 in the afternoon.
D. Every child here is sure to succeed.
E. The school has 30 computers for pupils to use.

boxes.title: A model: fact or opinion?
lines: Sunrise Academy opened in 2015: this is a fact, because you could check the date.
Sunrise Academy is the best school in Hargeisa: this is an opinion, because other people could disagree.
Both sentences are about the same school. The difference is only whether they can be checked.
Then think about your own school. Write down two facts about it, and one opinion. Notice how different they feel.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your six answers to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Then read your two facts and one opinion about your own school.
Ask the tutor: why does the advert use so many opinions that sound like promises?

activities.title: Match each source to the right question
activities.label: Activity 3: Match each source to the right question
activities.intro:
Your class is researching schools in another country. Here are four questions. Match each source (1 to 5) to the question (a to d) it answers. One source does not answer any of them — find the source that is not relevant.

The questions are: (a) At what age do children start school? (b) At what age do children leave school? (c) How many hours a week are children in school? (d) What time does the school day start and end?

Write the pairs, such as 1-a. Then write which source is not relevant, and one sentence saying how you knew.
steps: 'Starting School in Kenya' — In Kenya, most children begin primary school at the age of six.
'The School Week in Japan' — Children in Japan spend about thirty hours a week in class.
'A School Day in India' — The school day often begins at eight in the morning and ends at two.
'Leaving School Around the World' — In many countries, children may leave school at the age of sixteen.
'The Best Football Teams in the World' — Fans love to argue about which team is the greatest ever.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your pairs to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Tell it which source was not relevant, and how you knew.
Then ask: which of these sources matches something I would like to know, and why?

activities.title: Which source is the most useful?
activities.label: Activity 4: Which source is the most useful?
activities.intro: A learner wants to find out the truth about class size — how many children are in a class. She finds three sources online. Read them, then decide which is the most useful, and why.
steps: Who made each source, and why might they have made it?
Which source gives real evidence you can check, and which gives mostly opinions?
Which source is the most useful for finding the truth about class size? Give your reason.
Is there any source here that is only trying to sell something? Which one, and how do you know?

boxes.title: The three sources, described
lines: Source 1: Bright Star School's own web page. It says: small classes are best, and no class here is bigger than fifteen children!
Source 2: a teachers' opinion site. It says: most teachers believe smaller classes help — but is this really true?
Source 3: a statistics website. It shows the real average class size in many different countries.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your four answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether it would choose the same most-useful source as you.
Then ask the tutor: could the school's own page still be useful in any way?

activities.title: Two perspectives, and your own opinion
activities.label: Activity 5: Two perspectives, and your own opinion
activities.intro: Two newspapers print different views on what time school should start. A perspective is a way of seeing something. Read both, then give your own opinion with a reason.
steps: Who supports each start time, and what evidence does each one give?
Which perspective do you agree with more? Give one clear reason.
What evidence would you look for to be really sure?
Now think of one thing you would change about a school near you. Write what you would change, why, and what the result would be.

boxes.title: Two head teachers speak
lines: Green Hill School: We start at 7:15 in the morning. We have had no complaints in years.
Riverside School: We start at 10 in the morning. Students and teachers welcome it, and the place feels full of life.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your opinion on school start time, with your reason.
Ask it to argue the other side as strongly as it can.
Then tell the tutor your idea for changing a local school, and ask if your reason is clear and your result makes sense.

boxes.title: Bring it to your teacher
lines: Save your idea for changing a local school: what you would change, why, and the result.
Share it in your next teacher session, and hear how other learners would change their school.

activities.title: Choose the best book by its blurb
activities.label: Activity 6: Choose the best book by its blurb
activities.intro:
The author is the person who made a source. A blurb is the few sentences on the back of a book that tell you about it. A learner is researching fair access to computers in schools. Read the three blurbs, then choose the most useful book.

Write which book is the most relevant for the computer question, and why. Then write one thing the retired teacher's book might still be good for, and one thing it might not tell you.
steps: 'My Fifty Years in the Classroom' — a retired teacher shares memories of a long life teaching.
'Computers and Learning: What the Research Shows' — an education researcher studies how new technology helps children learn.
'Wild Rivers and Green Forests' — a journalist writes about nature and the environment.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your choice and your reason to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether the author's job makes a book more trustworthy for this question.
Then ask: for my own Challenge, who would be the best author to trust, and why?

activities.title: Useful or not useful for taking action?
activities.label: Activity 7: Useful or not useful for taking action?
activities.intro: Sometimes people want to do something, not just know about it. A school is half-closed for building work, so children study at home two days a week. Some parents want to act. Judge each source below as useful or not useful for those parents.
steps: A. A newspaper report called 'Home or School?' that looks at the real issue and gives facts and views.
B. Adverts for home tutoring that offer to sell extra lessons.
C. A leisure-centre website that lists swimming times.
Write useful or not useful next to A, B and C, with a short reason for each.
Which source would you trust most, and which least?
In the newspaper report, underline (or write down) one fact and one opinion you would expect to find.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three judgements to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether the tutoring adverts might be a little biased, and why.
Then ask the tutor to help you spot a fact and an opinion in one of your own Challenge sources.

activities.title: For or against? Who thinks that, and why?
activities.label: Activity 8: For or against? Who thinks that, and why?
activities.intro: On many issues, some people are for an idea and some are against it. Read what different people say about wearing a school uniform. Sort each one, and work out who might say it and why.
steps: A. I sell uniforms in my clothes shop.
B. I love choosing my own clothes to show who I am.
C. Chasing the latest fashions costs too much and wastes clothes.
D. Our uniform shows off our school wherever pupils go.
E. Young people should learn to choose sensible clothes for themselves.
Write FOR or AGAINST uniform next to each letter.
For each one, write who might say it, such as a shop owner, a parent, or a pupil.
For each one, write why they might hold that view.
Now give your own opinion about school uniform, with one clear reason.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your sorting and your ideas about who says each one to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your reasons make sense.
Then tell the tutor your own opinion, and ask it to challenge you with the opposite view.

activities.title: Read two parents' letters
activities.label: Activity 9: Read two parents' letters
activities.intro: When you say what you think of someone's idea, be exact: say what you agree or disagree with, and why. Two parents write to the school about the two-days-a-week home-study plan. Read each letter's ideas, then answer.
steps: For each letter, write the writer's opinion, their main reason, and their evidence.
Say what you agree with, and what you disagree with, and give a reason for each.
How do you think the school should reply to both parents fairly?

boxes.title: The two letters, in short
lines: Mr Adams thinks the plan is unfair. His main reason: his daughter has no computer at home. His evidence: she fell behind last term.
Mrs Silva likes the plan. Her main reason: her son concentrates better at home. Her evidence: his reading improved.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether you said exactly what you agree and disagree with, and gave a reason.
Then ask the tutor to be one of the parents, so you can practise replying kindly and clearly.

activities.title: Strengths, limitations and trust
activities.label: Activity 10: Strengths, limitations and trust
activities.intro: A strong evaluation names both what a source is good at and what it cannot do. Read the ideas from an author writing about learning at home. Sort each idea into strengths or limitations.
steps: A. Computers let us learn anywhere — you cannot deny it.
B. The writer says children learn by playing, but never says how or why.
C. The writer says classrooms are old-fashioned, but that is too general.
D. The writer gives real examples from three different schools.
Write strength or limitation next to A, B, C and D.
Now take two of your own Challenge sources. For each, write one strength and one limitation.
Decide which of your two sources is more trustworthy, and give your reason.
Think about the clever surprise from the Lesson: could a source you do not fully trust still be useful? Give one example.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your sorting of A to D to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Then read the strengths and limitations of your two sources.
Ask the tutor: which of my two sources should I trust more, and could the other one still be useful?

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 14 questions. Do not worry if some are tricky. Try each one before you look at the answer key, and use your own words.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'evaluation' mean?
practice.answer: Evaluation means thinking carefully about a source to decide how useful and trustworthy it is. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: Something that can be checked and shown to be true is called a ______.
practice.answer: A fact.

practice.prompt: What someone thinks or believes, which others may not agree with, is called an ______.
practice.answer: An opinion.

practice.prompt: The person or group who made a source is called the ______.
practice.answer: The author (or creator).

practice.prompt: The reason someone made a source is called its ______.
practice.answer: Its purpose.

practice.prompt: Fact or opinion? 'Sunrise Academy opened in the year 2015.'
practice.answer: A fact. You could check the date.

practice.prompt: Fact or opinion? 'Sunrise Academy is the best school in Hargeisa.'
practice.answer: An opinion. Other people could disagree.

practice.prompt: If a source is really about the question you are working on, we say it is ______.
practice.answer: Relevant.

practice.prompt: True or false: an advert's main purpose is usually to persuade you or sell you something.
practice.answer: True. An advert is usually made to persuade you or sell you something.

practice.prompt: The things a source is good at are its strengths. The things it is not good at are its ______.
practice.answer: Its limitations.

practice.prompt: A source you can believe, because it is fair and made by someone who knows, is ______.
practice.answer: Trustworthy.

practice.prompt: True or false: a source you cannot fully trust can never be useful for anything.
practice.answer: False. A source you cannot fully trust can still be useful, for example to show you a perspective or how someone tries to persuade.

practice.prompt: When you give your opinion about someone else's idea, you should always give a ______.
practice.answer: A reason.

practice.prompt: Name one question you can ask to help you decide if you can trust a source.
practice.answer: Any one of: who made it? why did they make it? does it give evidence I can check? is it fair, or does the maker have something to gain?

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each evaluation word (1 to 6) to the correct meaning (A to F). Write the pairs, such as 1-C.
practice.prompt: Source
options: A. Something that can be checked and shown to be true.
B. Anywhere your information comes from, like a book, advert or person.
C. The things a source is not good at, or cannot tell you.
D. Really about the question or issue you are working on.
E. What someone thinks or believes; others may not agree.
F. The things a source is good at, or does well.
practice.answer: B — Anywhere your information comes from, like a book, advert or person.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Fact
practice.answer: A — Something that can be checked and shown to be true.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Opinion
practice.answer: E — What someone thinks or believes; others may not agree.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Strengths
practice.answer: F — The things a source is good at, or does well.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Limitations
practice.answer: C — The things a source is not good at, or cannot tell you.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Relevant
practice.answer: D — Really about the question or issue you are working on.

practice.intro: These short questions ask you to use what you learned. Write a sentence or two for each.
practice.prompt: Amara finds a leaflet with no author's name and no date. Should she trust it fully? Explain, using the word author.
practice.answer: No. With no author, Amara cannot tell who made it or whether they know the topic, so she cannot be sure it is fair. She should find a source with a named author who knows the subject.

practice.prompt: Malik has an advert from a juice company, and a farming website about how mangoes grow. Which should he trust more for facts, and why?
practice.answer: The farming website, because it gives facts about how mangoes grow, while the juice advert is biased, as the company wants to sell the drink.

practice.prompt: Nadia reads that a juice is 'the healthiest drink ever'. Is that a fact or an opinion, and how do you know?
practice.answer: An opinion, because 'the healthiest drink ever' is what someone thinks, and others could disagree; it cannot be checked and proved.

practice.prompt: Omar says an advert is a great source of facts about a school. What is the problem with trusting an advert this way?
practice.answer: An advert's purpose is to persuade or sell, so it only shows the good side and hides anything unhelpful. It is not a fair source of facts about a school.

practice.prompt: Layla has a source she cannot fully trust: a biased juice advert. Could it still be useful to her in any way? Explain.
practice.answer: Yes, it could still be useful. Even though it is biased, it shows Layla how sellers try to make a sugary drink look healthy, which is a perspective worth understanding.

reflection.prompt: Working on my own, at my own speed ...
Working with my AI tutor, my partner and my class ...
Working with my teacher in live sessions ...
Asking someone at home about the food I eat ...

vocabulary.meaning: The reasons someone gives to try to make you agree with them.
The facts or proof that show whether something is true.
Something that can be checked and shown to be true.
Facts and details about a topic.
The things a source is not good at, or cannot tell you.
What someone thinks or believes; other people may not agree.
The different ways people see or think about something.
Thinking about how you learn and how your ideas have changed.
Really about the question or issue you are working on.
Finding out about a topic in a careful, organised way.
Anywhere your information comes from: a person, book, website, advert or video.
The things a source is good at, or does well.
To back up an idea or an action with good reasons or evidence.
The person or group who made a source; also called the creator.
The reason someone made a source; what they want it to do.
To give people facts and help them understand.
To try to make people agree, or do or buy something.
It helps you with the question or the job you are working on.
You can believe it, because it is fair and made by someone who knows.
Thinking carefully about a source to decide how useful and trustworthy it is.

mistakes: Calling a source just 'good' or 'bad' instead of asking 'useful for what?'.
Trusting a source just because it looks bright, or comes first in a list.
Forgetting to check who made a source, and why.
Believing an advert as if it were a fair source of facts.
Naming only strengths, or only limitations, instead of both.
Mixing up a fact with an opinion.
Giving an opinion with no reason.

selfAssessment.statement: I can talk about a source and the ideas it gives about an issue.
I can give reasons for my opinion about an issue.
I can tell a fact from an opinion in a source.
I can say whether a source is relevant to my question.
I can say which source is the most useful, and why.
I can talk about who made a source and why they made it.
I can give my perspective on other people's ideas, with reasons.
I can name some strengths and limitations of a source.
I can decide which of two sources is more trustworthy.
